missing_spec_content.spec_text: explain methods used to measure human reaction times and recall typical results
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives the typical range of 0.2–0.9 s. It never explains how reaction time is measured, for example the ruler-drop test or a computer-based test.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: interpret and evaluate measurements from simple methods to measure the different reaction times of students
missing_spec_content.why: There are no reaction-time measurements to interpret or evaluate, and repeat readings, averages and variation between students are not discussed.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: evaluate the effect of various factors on thinking distance based on given data.
missing_spec_content.why: Factors are listed descriptively. The student is never asked to evaluate their effect from given data.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (Physics only) Students will be required to interpret graphs relating speed to stopping distance for a range of vehicles.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson has a car-only table and no speed–stopping distance graph. It does not cover other vehicles such as lorries or bicycles.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson presents speed only as increasing braking distance at constant force. It never states this converse relationship.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control.
missing_spec_content.why: Overheating and forces on passengers are covered. Loss of control (for example skidding when the wheels lock) is not mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) estimate the forces involved in the deceleration of road vehicles in typical situations on a public road.
missing_spec_content.why: F = ma is quoted, but there is no worked estimate using typical car mass, speed and deceleration.

above_gcse.text: The UK legal minimum tyre tread depth is 1.6 mm.
above_gcse.why: This is a legal detail that the specification does not require. It is not physics content.

above_gcse.text: severe tiredness can cause microsleep at the wheel
above_gcse.why: Microsleep is not in the specification. It adds a term the student does not need.

above_gcse.text: Age: reaction times tend to slow with age
above_gcse.why: The specification lists only tiredness, drugs, alcohol and distractions. Adding age to a list the lesson presents as the key factors may lead students to give it as an answer the specification does not name.
Brake fade is not a specification term. The specification only requires 'brakes overheating'.

factual_errors.text: That is roughly four car-lengths compared with 24 car-lengths.
factual_errors.correction: The standard Highway Code comparison is about 6 car-lengths at 30 mph (23 m) and 24 car-lengths at 70 mph (96 m). 'Four' is inconsistent with the 24 car-lengths for 96 m, because it implies a different car length.

factual_errors.text: The force applied by the brakes to decelerate the vehicle; transferred from kinetic energy to thermal energy in the brakes
factual_errors.correction: A force is not transferred between energy stores. The work done by the friction force reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and increases the temperature of the brakes.

factual_errors.text: This is because kinetic energy = ½mv², and braking distance is proportional to KE.
factual_errors.correction: Braking distance is proportional to KE only for a given (constant) braking force. The specification states the speed link 'For a given braking force'.

factual_errors.text: slows brain processing significantly — the biggest single impairment
factual_errors.correction: Nothing supports ranking alcohol as the single biggest impairment. The specification lists tiredness, drugs and alcohol without ranking them, and the effect depends on the amount.

factual_errors.text: Ice can reduce friction to nearly zero.
factual_errors.correction: Ice greatly reduces friction, but the friction between tyres and ice is still well above zero. 'Nearly zero' is an exaggeration.

wrong_terms.text: The kinetic energy of the car is transferred to thermal energy (heat) in the brakes through friction.
wrong_terms.spec_term: work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel ... the temperature of the brakes increases

wrong_terms.text: Kinetic energy transferred to thermal energy (heat) in the brakes
wrong_terms.spec_term: the temperature of the brakes increases (thermal energy, not 'heat')

wrong_terms.text: worn tyres have less tread → less grip → less braking force

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: checkpoints.1: A car's braking distance at 20 m/s is 25 m. What would the braking distance be at 40 m/s, on the same road?
checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[1].heading: Factors affecting reaction time and thinking distance
checkpoint_mismatch.why: This checkpoint tests the quadratic link between speed and braking distance, which is taught in keyPoints[2]. It does not test the reaction-time factors in the key point it sits with, and no checkpoint tests reaction-time factors at all.
